```{r options, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7,
                      fig.height = 4.5, fig.align = "center", dpi = 96)
old_options <- options(digits = 4, width = 100)
```

Latent transition analysis (LTA) estimates the probability of moving from one
latent profile to another between consecutive occasions (Collins & Lanza,
2010). With group classes, each class has its own starting distribution and its
own transition matrix, so the classes separate students who differ in how their
engagement changes from students who differ only in where it starts.

## Data and model

`engagement_momentum` holds 1,310 course enrolments of 106 students, ordered
within each student by `sequence`. The five indicators are simulated as
continuous values on a log-activity scale and standardized within course. The
data are synthetic and follow the design of the engagement studies of Saqr and
López-Pernas (2021) and López-Pernas and Saqr (2024), which identified
course-level engagement states with latent class analysis and followed
students' sequences of states across a program. In the simulation, each
student follows one of three trajectories (engaged, fluctuating or mostly
disengaged), each a first-order Markov chain over three engagement states
(active, average and disengaged). Engaged students show momentum, in that an
active course tends to be followed by another active course; mostly disengaged
students show inertia, in that a disengaged course tends to be followed by
another disengaged course. Three profiles and three student classes therefore
match the structure from which the data were generated, and the
[evaluation vignette](case-engagement-evaluation.html) shows that the BIC selects the same numbers for the multilevel profile model.

For student $i$ at course position $t$, $C_{it}$ is the latent profile and
$G_i$ the student's class. The model estimates

- the initial probabilities $\delta_{k\mid m}=P(C_{i1}=k\mid G_i=m)$,
- the transition probabilities
  $a_{kl\mid m}=P(C_{i,t+1}=l\mid C_{it}=k,G_i=m)$, which sum to one across
  destinations $l$,
- and a Gaussian mean and variance for each profile and indicator.

The transitions are first order and homogeneous: the next profile depends only
on the current profile and the student's class, and the probabilities are the
same at every position. Profile means and variances are shared across positions
and classes, so a change of profile is a change of state. Indicators are
independent within a profile under the default diagonal covariance. The fit can
fail to reach the global maximum from a single start, and a transition that is
rare within a class is estimated from little information; the expected count
of each transition shows how much.

```{r fit}
library(latents)
vars <- c("browse", "lectures", "forum_read", "forum_post", "active_days")

moves <- lta(engagement_momentum, vars, "student", n_profiles = 3,
             n_group_classes = 3, time = "sequence", n_starts = 10, seed = 1)
get_results(moves, "starts")
```

All ten starts converge to the same log likelihood, so the solution is
replicated within this seed's starts. The warning reports that one estimated
probability lies at its numerical boundary; the section on sparse and boundary
estimates below identifies it.

## The profiles

`plot_profiles()` draws the profile means across the indicators, and each
line's label gives the profile's share of the enrolments.

```{r profiles}
plot_profiles(moves)
```

```{r profile-means}
get_results(moves)
```

Profile 1 is the disengaged state, Profile 2 the average state and Profile 3
the active state, with means of days active of -0.960, 0.005 and 0.790
standard deviations from the course mean. The heatmap shows the same means as
standard deviations from each indicator's grand mean.

```{r heatmap}
plot_profiles(moves, what = "heatmap")
```

The contrast between profiles is present on all five indicators, so the
profiles differ in overall activity more than in its composition.

## Where students start

In the `"initial"` table, `probability` is $\delta_{k\mid m}$, the chance of
starting in each profile. `prevalence` is the expected share of all of a
class's enrolments in that profile, across the whole history, and
`group_class_probability` is the share of students in the class.

```{r initial}
get_results(moves, "initial")
```

Student class 1, with 21.8% of students, starts in the disengaged profile
with probability 0.746, and 0.821 of its enrolments are expected there over
the whole history. Class 3, with 44.1% of students, starts in the active
profile with probability 0.613, and 0.688 of its enrolments are expected
there. Class 2, with 34.1% of students, starts across all three profiles, with
probabilities 0.383, 0.367 and 0.250, and spends its enrolments in similar
proportions. Class 1 is therefore the mostly disengaged class, class 2 the
fluctuating class and class 3 the engaged class. In classes 1 and 3, the
expected share of enrolments in the dominant profile exceeds the probability
of starting there: over the program, students drift towards the state that
their class favours.

## How engagement changes

The `"transitions"` table gives $a_{kl\mid m}$ for every class and pair of
profiles. `stable` marks staying in the same profile. `expected_count` is the
posterior expected number of such transitions in the data, so it can be
fractional, and it shows how much information supports each estimate.
`estimated = FALSE` would mark a row the data cannot inform, because the
profile is never occupied before a student's last course; such a row holds
uniform placeholder values. Every row is estimated in this fit.

```{r transitions}
get_results(moves, "transitions")
```

The transition plot draws each class's matrix as a heatmap, with the origin
profile in rows and the destination in columns.

```{r transition-plot}
plot_transitions(moves)
```

In class 1, a disengaged course is followed by another disengaged course with
probability 0.904, estimated from 196 expected transitions, and an average
course is followed by a disengaged one with probability 0.617 (from 34.7
expected transitions): disengagement
has inertia, and the average state leads back into it. In class 3, an active
course is followed by another active course with probability 0.808, estimated
from 297 expected transitions, and an average course is followed by an active
one with probability 0.473: engagement has momentum. Class 2 has no dominant
transition; its largest probability, 0.566, takes an active course to an
average one, and its other probabilities lie between 0.20 and 0.44. These are
the patterns of the generating model, in which disengagement and activity
persist with probability 0.85 in the corresponding trajectories, and the
fluctuating trajectory moves between states with probabilities between 0.25
and 0.40.

## Sparse and boundary estimates

Some estimates rest on little information. Students in class 1 rarely occupy
the active profile, so its transitions out of the active profile rest on 16.0
expected transitions and those out of the average profile on 34.7. Its
probability of moving from the average to the active profile is at its lower
bound, which is why Wald inference is withheld for this fit. A probability
near zero shows that the data carry little information about that movement,
not that the movement is impossible: in the generating model, mostly
disengaged students move from the average to the active state with
probability 0.10. Estimates like these can also mean that the chosen number of
classes divides the available transitions too finely.

## Assigned sequences

The sequence plot shows each student's modal profile at each course position,
one row per student. Modal assignment discards classification uncertainty.

```{r sequences, fig.height = 6}
plot_sequences(moves)
```

```{r sequence-summary}
get_results(moves, "sequence_summary")
```

The summary gives the number of students and courses in each assigned class:
22 students with 278 courses in class 1, 39 with 473 in class 2 and 45 with
559 in class 3. Sequence lengths range from 10 to 15 courses, so the rows of
the plot end at different positions. The long runs of the disengaged profile
in class 1 and of the active profile in class 3 are the inertia and momentum
of the transition table, seen in the individual histories.

## Classification uncertainty

```{r entropy-table}
get_results(moves, "entropy")
```

Relative entropy is 0.825 for enrolments and 0.774 for students. The entropy
plot shows, within each profile, how the per-case entropy contributions are
distributed, and the posterior plot shows the posterior probability of each
case's assigned profile.

```{r entropy-plot}
plot_diagnostics(moves, what = "entropy")
```

```{r posteriors-plot}
plot_diagnostics(moves, what = "posteriors")
```

Both levels retain uncertainty, so an analysis that replaces the posteriors by
modal assignments treats some enrolments and students as more certain than
the model estimates them to be.

## Transition networks

`get_tna()` returns the marginal transition matrix as a model of the tna
package (Tikka et al., 2025). It pools the posterior expected transition counts
across classes and normalizes them, so it uses the estimated transitions, not
transitions counted from modal assignments. `get_group_tna()` returns one
network per class.

```{r network, message = FALSE}
network <- get_tna(moves)
plot(network)
```

```{r group-network, message = FALSE, fig.height = 4}
per_class <- get_group_tna(moves)
plot(per_class)
```

The class networks show the patterns of the transition table: a dominant
self-loop on the disengaged profile in class 1, movement among all three
profiles in class 2, and a dominant self-loop on the active profile in
class 3.

## Recovery of the generating structure

The same check against the generating states and trajectories as in the
[introductory vignette](case-engagement-profiles.html) applies to the
transition model.

```{r recovery}
get_results(moves, "assignments", data = engagement_momentum,
            truth = c("state", "trajectory"))
```

The transition model recovers the states as well as the multilevel profile
model does: 93.3%, 79.9% and 95.4% of the active, average and disengaged
enrolments, against 92.9%, 79.9% and 94.7%. It recovers the engaged and mostly
disengaged trajectories about as well (88.4% and 90.9%, against 86.0% and
90.9%), but the fluctuating trajectory less well (80.5%, against 95.1%).

## Limitations

The model assumes constant transition probabilities across course positions,
so change specific to one stage of the program is averaged over positions; the
simulated data satisfy this assumption, but applied data need not.
Transitions are between successive observed courses, which can differ in
duration, content and assessment. Class differences describe patterns in
engagement histories and do not identify their causes. Wald standard errors
are withheld for this fit because class 1's probability of moving from the
average to the active profile sits at its lower bound, and the numbers of
profiles and classes were not compared for the transition model here;
`enumerate_classes()` with `time` compares transition models over a grid of
profile and class counts. Transitions supported by few expected counts, such
as those out of the active profile in class 1, should not be interpreted.
